Effect of nutrient solution and Martian regolith simulant on the growth and 
development of lettuce (Lactuca sativa) Rhodenas RZ (45-113) 
Coral Martinez-Nolasco1, Armando Figueroa-Martinez1, Karla Mendoza-Ramos1, Raul A. Munoz-Gutierrez1, 
Mauricio Erazo-Barradas2 
1 Tecnologico Nacional de Mexico-Celaya 
2 Tarleton State University, Texas, USA 
 
Keywords / Martian regolith, Nutrient solution, Organic amendments, Lettuce, Organic matter, IoT 
1. Introduction 
Farming on Mars in the current environment provides challenge opportunities 
because these activities would have to occur in habitats that could provide an adequate 
temperature, radiation and water (Yamashita, et al., 2009). Such habitats would need to be 
transparent to let in sunlight for plants to grow or would have to come equipped with lights 
to sustain plant growth (Poulet et al., 2014). Data returned from various missions to Mars 
indicate that the Martian “soil” has some essential nutrients, but is often rocky, coarse, and 
deficient in organic matter and other important nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorous, and 
sulfur (Chinnannan et al., 2024). Even so, previous studies have reported the use of simulant 
soils for Mars showing that plants can germinate and grow, albeit not as vigorously as on 
Earth. Earlier studies have established the capacity of specific regolith simulants to support 
the growth of a variety of plants in the short term (Wamelink et al., 2014). However, the 
mineralogical and physical accuracy of these simulants as proxies for the sites on Mars is 
debatable, and any conclusion drawn from studies with these simulants must be considered 
with some degree of caution. Therefore, plant growth could be facilitated by addition of 
fertilizers, soil amendments and nutrient solutions (Duri et al., 2022). Based on the 
aforementioned, the hypothesis proposed in this study was that the application of nutrient 
solution at different concentrations to a variety of lettuce established in different physical soil 
mixtures had an effect on the time required to reach the different phenological stages of the 
crop which will affect biomass production and yield. 
The objective of this study was to quantify the combined effect of a nutrient solution 
applied at different concentrations to the physical mixture of Martian simulant (regolith) and 
soil amendments (coconut fiber, vermiculite, perlite and peat moss) on the growth stages and 
yield of lettuce.The objective of this study was to quantify the combined effect of a nutrient 
solution applied at different concentrations to the physical mixture of Martian simulant 
(regolith) and soil amendments (coconut fiber, vermiculite, perlite and peat moss) on the 
growth stages and yield of lettuce. 
 
2. Literature Review 
According to NASA, it is believed that the first continually inhabited Martian colony will be 
established by 2050. Assuming that the challenges associated with the Martian environment, 
its distance from Earth, and how to sustain life in Mars are addressed properly, the success 
will depend on identifying and resolving these issues prior to the start of such a mission 
(Neukart, 2024). From the standpoint of human beings’ ability to survive and thrive in such 
as harsh conditions of Mars, an emerging and critical theme in environmental system

management in agriculture is sustainability, or the ability to maintain existing production 
from an ecological system, while ensuring its ability and availability at a future date (Gaffney 
et al., 2019). Besides being crucial to the success in the long term on Earth at maintaining 
food security and ecosystem viability, sustainable systems of agriculture production on Mars 
must be able to provide all the elements necessary for future missions in the quest for 
colonizing this planet. 
Another crucial aspect of off-world sustainability effort is a dependency on in-situ Resource 
Utilization (ISRU), or the use of existing materials at the site whenever possible. ISRU will 
allow colonists to introduce new materials into their closed-loop ecosystem without relying 
solely on resupply missions. On Mars, examples of in situ resources will include water, light, 
regolith, and perchlorates for oxygen as well as harnessing the CO2 in the atmosphere to 
introduce new biomass for food production. Plant growth systems utilizing Martian regolith, 
could influence the advances of sustainable agriculture systems to limit fertilizer use, 
improve disease resistance, and build viable nutrient cycling systems that augment existing 
life support systems. Indeed, food security alone will demand the presence of multiple 
sources of food production, including a traditional agriculture approach alongside 
hydroponics, aquaponics, and others ((Wheeler, 2010). 
Recent studies have mentioned that there is a need for developing regolith-based plant growth 
systems for Mars and its importance depends upon on the quality of the Martian regolith 
simulant (MRS) used (Peters et al., 2008). As a result, the process of understanding the 
limitations of this materials should be iterative, with new simulants being developed as our 
knowledge of the Martian surface improves. Finally, the presence of organic matter is not 
required to support plant growth, but typically improves the texture, cation exchange capacity 
(CEC), water holding capacity (WHC), and other properties of a soil which may provide an 
additional pool for nutrients providing a more fertile growth medium. Organic matter is 
extremely low in Martian regolith and bedrock and this may decrease its potential as a fertile 
medium. 
 
3. Materials and Methods 
3.1 Growth chamber experiment. 
The experiment began on September 30, 2024 and ended with the harvest on November 
23, 2024. It took place in a growth chamber equipped within the National Technology of 
Mexico in Celaya, campus 2. The stages of the methodology were: Design of experiments, 
conditioning of growth chamber, preparation of pots and planting, crop monitoring and 
harvest.

Figura 1. Graphic summary of the methodology developed 
 
3.1.1 Temperature 
The temperature inside the room was provided by a Minisplit Mirage Magnum 22 Hot/Cold 
Inverter 1.5ton air conditioner, which seeks to have temperatures between 25 to 27 °C. 
 
3.1.2 Relative humidity 
The relative humidity was set between 60% to 80%, to help achieve the desired range of 
humidity inside the room an automatic humidifier was installed. 
 
3.1.3 Lightning 
Artificial lighting was supplied by Barrina LED grow lights that provided light infinitely 
close to the natural light spectrum. From day two to day four after sowing, the lighting was 
kept constant at 100 µmol*m-2*s-1, from day 5 until the day of harvest the lightning was at 
200 µmol*m-2*s-1; this light setting provided a daily photoperiod of 16 hours. 
3.1.4 Crop structure 
A cultivation structure measuring 1.2 x 0.8 meters x 1.75 meters high was built, with 5 lines 
of LED lamps on the top, the purpose of the structure was to place the pots. On November 7, 
38 days after sowing, a second floor was built in the structure since the lettuces no longer 
had enough space for their development. 
3.2 Nutrient solution 
A Universal Steiner nutrient solution (Steiner, 1961) will be used to prepare the levels of the 
nutrient factor. The nutrient solution is composed of essential inorganic macronutrients and

micronutrients to maintain overal health and performance of the lettuce. The nutrient 
composition of the solution is: N, P, K, Ca, Mg, S, Fe-EDTA, Cu, Zn-EDTA, Mn-EDTA, B, 
Mo, and Fe-EDTA. The commercial Steiner-type nutrient solutions A and B, both solutions 
are prepared separately and mixed at the final concentration. The nutrient solution was 
prepared using water with a pH between the range 5.5 to 6.5. To reduce the pH of the drinking 
water in our location, which generally ranges from 8, 2 ml of nitric acid is added per liter of 
water. Initially, stock solutions A and B are prepared to later dilute the experiment 
concentrations. The 100% nutrient solution concentration contains 5 ml of solution A and 5 
ml of solution B, the other concentrations are prepared proportionally, that is, 75% contains 
3.75 ml A and 3.75 ml B and 50% contains 2.5 ml A and 2.5 ml B, respectively. The nutrient 
solution was monitored with an All Dissolved Solids meter, the measurements for each 
concentration were: for 100% the pH is 6, the electrical conductivity (EC) = 1970 µS/cm and 
TDS = 985 ppm, for 75 % the pH is 5.83, the EC = 1621 µS/cm and TDS = 810, for 50% the 
pH is 5.93, electrical conductivity (EC) = 1272 µS/cm and TDS = 636 ppm. 
3.3 Sowing 
Seeds of Rhodenas RZ (45-113), a round-shaped iceberg lettuce variety, adapted to temperate 
areas of outdoor production, were buried into the soil mixture approximately 0.5 cm Deep. 
The seeds were covered with vermiculite and watered at field capacity with water at pH 6. 
The top portion of the pot was covered with aluminum foil to ensure darkness for the seed, 
and it was placed inside the growth chamber at 25 °C. After 24 hours, the presence of the 
first sprung was checked in each pot/treatment in order to determine the germination of the 
seed and if the seed has already sprung so, the temperature was increased to 27 °C, the pot 
was uncovered and it was switched to an artificial lighting system at 100 µmol*m-2. *s-1, 
the appearance of cotyledons is expected around 72 hours after sowing, at which time the 
artificial lighting was increased to 200 µmol*m-2*s-1, the other variables remained the same. 
Once the first true leaf appeared, the administration of the Steiner-type nutrient solution, 
prepared with pH 6, begins (Figure 2).

3.4 Monitoring of variables through the Internet of Things (IoT) 
The design and implementation of an IoT system for the growth chamber has made it possible 
to guarantee optimal control of critical environmental variables: temperature, relative 
humidity, lighting and carbon dioxide (CO2). This system was developed with the aim of 
automating and monitoring the internal conditions of the camera by using sensors, actuators 
and reliable communication protocols, managed by an Arduino Mega in conjunction with an 
ESP-32 board for connection to the cloud. 
 
First, temperature and humidity, critical for the development of organisms in the 
chamber, were controlled by a combined temperature and humidity sensor that continuously 
measured internal conditions. The system used an air conditioner as an actuator for 
temperature regulation, while a humidifier was responsible for maintaining humidity within 
optimal ranges. Both functions were managed by the Arduino Mega, which analyzes the 
sensor readings and activates the corresponding actuators in real time, ensuring a stable and 
suitable environment for the lettuce. 
 
The monitoring and control of carbon dioxide (CO2) was also an essential component of 
the system, since this gas is essential for plant photosynthesis. A specialized sensor measured 
the CO2 concentration in parts per million (ppm) inside the chamber. 
 
Regarding lighting, the system was calibrated with a photosynthetic active radiation 
(PAR) sensor to measure the light intensity in the environment and ensure that the radiation 
was at optimal value for the different stages of lettuce growth. 
To ensure efficient communication between system components, the RS-485 protocol 
was used, which connected the sensors to the Arduino Mega. This protocol was selected for 
its robustness, reliability, and ability to handle interference in controlled environments.

Subsequently, the data processed by the Arduino Mega was sent to an ESP-32 board via serial 
communication. The ESP-32 acts as an intermediary, sending the collected information to 
the cloud through the HTTP protocol. 
 
Finally, once in the cloud, the data was stored and managed on the ThingSpeak platform, 
which organized it into interactive graphs and panels accessible from any mobile device. 
Users could view real-time temperature, humidity, CO2 and lighting readings, allowing for 
constant remote monitoring of the growth chamber status. 
 
 
 
Figura 3. Resumen gráfico de la metodología desarrollada 
 
3.5.1 Temperature and Relative humidity 
 
Temperature and relative humidity are artificially manipulated and priority variables for 
optimal crop development. Both variables are monitored by sensors. JXBS-3001-TH-RS is 
the sensor used for both variables. The data collected from the sensors is continuous, 
however, the data collected is sent to the cloud with a sampling period of 5 minutes. The 
results of minimum, maximum temperature and relative humidity during the 54 days of 
cultivation are shown in Figure 4.

Figure 4. Temperature and relative humidity during the cultivation experiment. 
 
 
3.5.2 Lightning and CO2 
 
The Flux of Photosynthetically Active Photons was monitored with the SEM228P sensor and 
the values are recorded by the IoT monitoring system. CO2 particles are recorded with the 
JXBS-3001-CO2-RS sensor, the measurement unit is parts per million ppm. The data was 
uploaded to the cloud every 5 minutes. The monitoring results are shown in Figure 5. 
 
 
 
 
Figure 5. CO2 particles and flow of photosynthetically active photons throughout IoT.

3.5 Experimental Design 
The experiment consisted of 9 treatments (Figure 1) arranged in a Factorial Completely 
Randomized Design (FCRD) with 4 replications. The treatments were formed by a 
combination of the three levels of soil mixture (M: M1 (50% regolith + 50% Soil 
amendments), M2 (75% regolith + 25% Soil amendments, M3 (100% regolith + 0 % Soil 
amendments) and three levels of Steiner-type (Steiner, 1984) nutrient solution (N: N1 
(100%), N2 (75%), N3 (50%)) (Table 2). The factorial treatment structure of this experiment 
is useful for examining the effects of these two factors on a response variable (Y), whether 
or not interaction exists. The linear statistical model for a FCRD is the following:

3.6 Variables 
3.6.1 Germination 
It was recorded as the number of days from sowing until the cotyledons were raised above 
the soil surface. This occurs when the hypocotyl, the region between the cotyledon and 
radicle, elongates rapidly and arches upward, pulling the cotyledon above the soil. 
3.6.2 Seedling 
The seedling stage was recorded as the number of the days from the appearance of the first 
true leaf until the plant developed a distinct circular cluster of leaves known as rosette. 
3.6.3 Rosette 
For this variable, the rosette formation was recorded as the number of days when at least six 
true-leaves were present forming a circular cluster. 
3.6.4 Plant height 
The plant height was measured in centimeters (cm) from the base of the stem (at the soil 
surface) to the top of the canopy, or the highest part of the plant (for many plants, this was 
the tip of the apical bud). This activity was performed twenty-one times evenly spaced 
throughout the duration of the experiment. Data from the average and final plant height were 
used to perform analyses of variance. 
3.6.5 Leaf area 
The leaf area was calculated in cm2, using digital image processing that was captured from 
the top view of the plant. During the duration of the experiment, 13 capture sessions were 
taken on each treatment/plant, distributed evenly during the 54 days that the research lasted. 
The image processing was carried out using Python language and libraries such as OpenCV. 
Data from the average and final leaf area were used to perform analyses of variance.

3.6.6 Number of leaves 
The number of leaves in each plant was manually collected twenty-one times evenly spaced 
throughout the duration of the experiment. Data from the average and final number of leaves 
were used to perform analyses of variance. 
3.6.7 Chlorophyll content 
The Chlorophyll content was measured manually with an Apogee MC-100 chlorophyll 
concentration meter (SPAD). Data collection was performed three times at 24, 37, and 54 
days after sowing on the same leaf of the treatment plants during the duration of the 
experiment. Chlorophyll content from the three dates and average were used to perform 
analyses of variance. 
3.6.8 Fresh weight 
Fresh weight also known as wet weight of lettuce was recorded in grams as the weight of 
lettuce measured immediately after harvest (54 days), this variable included the water content 
of the lettuce. Fresh weight is a common way to measure crop growth and is often used to 
evaluate yield results before selling produce. 
3.6.9 Dry weight 
The dry weight of lettuce is the weight of the lettuce after all of its water content has been 
removed through drying. The dry weight of lettuce was obtained by dehydrating the lettuce 
after being removed from the growth chamber. On harvest day the leaves were placed in 
individually labeled kraft bags. Subsequently, they were placed in a drying oven at a 
temperature of 71.8 °C for 72 hours. Immediately after being removed from the oven, the dry 
weight was manually recorded in grams. 
 
3.6.10 pH 
Soil pH was measured every week starting from week 2, after the application of the nutrient 
solution began, the measurement was done with pH measuring strips, at the end a soil pH 
measuring instrument was purchased. Data was collected on all 32 plants by placing the test 
strip in the drops of nutrient solution draining from the pot after watering. 
 
3.7 Statistical analysis 
Analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to analyze the collected data for the variables 
described. The linear statistical model for a Factorial Completely Randomized Design 
(FCRD) (Steel and Torrie, 1996) was used to analyze the data in this research. 
 
4. Results 
3.8 Phenological Variables 
Data of the physiological and morphometric parameters were analyzed using the Shapiro–
Wilk test with a value α = 0.05, and the normal distribution of the data was corroborated with 
minimum and maximum p-values obtained of 0.023 and 0.84, respectively. 
 
Statistical tests of differences in morphometric and physiological parameters of the 
different treatments were performed using two-way ANOVA. These analyzes were

performed with the R software (R Core Team, 2024) and the results were considered 
significantly different if p ≤ 0.05. The results showed that there were only significant 
differences for the variables fresh mass, final chlorophyll content and the average leaf area 
(Tables 2, 3, and 4).

For the variable germination, figure 7 shows the germination percentage that corresponded 
to each soil mixture in combination with the concentrations of the nutrient solution. Six 
combinations had 100% germination, 2 had 75% and the lowest was 50%, which corresponds 
to the mixture of 100% regolith soil with 50% nutrient solution.

Figure 7. Germination percentage per soil mix 
 
The total percentage of gemination for the experimental design was 88.9% corresponding to 
32 treatments, while the percentage of non-germination was 11.1%, which is equivalent to 4 
treatments (Figure 8). 
 
 
 
Figure 8. Total germination percentage

4.2 Watering 
In the present investigation, the irrigation variable was one of the most important, from the 
beginning, the irrigation was carried out manually with the use of a graduated pipette and at 
field soil capacity, initially the pots required 6.5 ml, from day 40 to 44 the plants required 
120 ml and after day 45 the requirement was 60 ml daily. The same amount of nutrient 
solution was applied to the pots of the 3 concentrations. Figure 9 shows the demand for 
nutrient solution by phenological stage. 
 
 
 
Figure 9. Germination percentage per soil mix

4.3 pH Measuring 
Figure 10 shows the pH of each treatment, as a consequence of the reaction of the soil 
mixture and the different concentrations of the nutrient solution. 
 
Figure 10. Average soil pH per treatment 
4.4 Phenological Stages of Lettuce 
Figure 11 shows the growth stages of a lettuce plant from sowing to harvest, detailing the 
days after sowing (DAS) in which each of these phases occur. In this research, all treatment 
combinations evaluated, the lettuce plants developed the stages shown in the Figure 11. 
.

Figure 11. Phenological stages for lettuce cultivation with different treatments 
 
4.5 Morphometric parameters 
The morphometric parameters of a lettuce plant are quantitative measurements used to 
describe its morphology or shape, size and structure. These parameters provide information 
about the growth, development and performance of the plant (Figure 12). The use of digital 
images has the advantage of being a non-destructive test that allows the crop to be monitored 
continuously.

Figure 12. Growing of a lettuce plant on different dates in one of the pots containing a 
treatment combination of soil mix and nutrient solution. 
 
The graph in Figure 13 shows the average area (cm²) of the plants throughout the days after 
sowing (DAS), according to different treatments. The average area of the first day was 0.88 
cm2 and the average of session 13 was 417.39 cm2. Growth is slower at the beginning (0-10 
DAS), followed by an accelerated increase starting at 20 DAS. Between 30 and 45 DAS, leaf 
areas tend to stabilize. M75N100 and M50N100 reach the largest average area, 
approximately 480 cm² at the end of the period (45 DAS). This indicates that combinations 
with high levels of N (100) and intermediate levels of M (50-75) favor leaf development. 
 
 
 
 
 
Figure 13. Average lettuce growing area under different treatments.

The graph (Fig 14) shows the average plant height (cm) as a function of days after sowing 
(DAS) for different treatments. Plant height increases gradually over time (from 10 to 40 
DAS), showing an initial exponential growth trend followed by a plateau phase. From day 
40 DAS, most treatments reach their maximum height and growth stabilizes. The M75N100 
treatment presents the greatest growth throughout the entire period, reaching approximately 
14 cm. In contrast, the M50N50 treatment shows the lowest growth, stabilizing near 12 cm. 
 
 
Figure 14. Average lettuce crop height under different treatments. 
 
5. Discussion & Conclusions 
In the development of this experiment, the germination stage has a crucial role; it is 
highlighted that the differences in the percentage of seed germination are a function of the 
combination of soil mixtures and nutrient solution concentrations. The results clearly show 
that the most optimal conditions were achieved in 6 combinations, where 100% germination 
was obtained. This suggests that these mixtures managed to meet the basic needs of the seeds 
in terms of nutrients and physical characteristics of the substrate. 
 
On the other hand, 2 combinations only reached 75% germination, which indicates that 
certain factors, such as the quantity of nutrients or the quality of the substrate, could have 
been limiting. Finally, the lowest percentage of germination (50%) occurred in the mixture 
of 100% Regolith soil with 50% nutrient solution. This reflects that a soil composed solely 
of regolith, combined with a low concentration of nutrients, is insufficient to support optimal 
initial seed development. 
 
According to the values obtained for leaf area, the combination that presents the lowest 
growth is M100N50 and the one that presents the highest growth is M75N100. In the plant

height analysis, the lowest combinations are at M100N50 and M50N50. Both parameters 
indicate that high concentrations of regolith with lower concentrations of nutrients do not 
favor crop growth. 
 
The results show that, although it is possible to achieve germination in simulated regolith 
soils, the combination of the substrate with an adequate nutrient solution is crucial. This 
highlights the need to enrich the Martian regolith through fertilizers or other strategies if it is 
to be used as a culture medium in future space missions.
